review_scope: Developer comparison of these bounded explanations with the cited source passages; no clinician or faculty review. Source wording concerns are tracked separately. This is paired approved text, not an automatic semantic verification system.

units.text: Osmosis is water moving through a membrane that lets water pass while limiting the movement of dissolved substances. Water moves down its own concentration gradient. Only water is moving by osmosis; the dissolved particles themselves are not being transported by osmosis. Aquaporins are channels that help water cross cell membranes.

Diffusion is the movement of a substance from an area where it is more concentrated to an area where it is less concentrated. The difference gradually becomes smaller. It is passive transport: the cell does not spend energy to drive this movement down the concentration gradient.

Homeostasis means keeping the body's internal conditions within a stable range. It does not mean everything stays at one fixed value. Cells and organs continually monitor conditions and make adjustments to keep important variables within ranges compatible with life.

Pharmacokinetics describes what happens to a medicine as it moves through the body. The four stages are absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion, often shortened to ADME. Absorption brings it from its administration site into the circulation; distribution carries it through the body; metabolism changes the drug molecule; excretion removes it or its breakdown products. Time is part of understanding this journey.

sources: The Relationship Between Pharmacokinetics and Pharmacodynamics
units.text: Pharmacodynamics describes the body's biological response to a medicine. Pharmacokinetics describes the medicine's movement through the body. These are connected ideas, but they answer different questions: where the drug goes, and what response it produces.

sources: Nephron Structure and Function / Function of a Nephron / Filtration
units.text: The glomerulus is the kidney's filtering structure. Pressure pushes water and small dissolved substances from its capillaries into the glomerular capsule; this fluid is called filtrate and then enters the renal tubule. Blood cells and proteins too large to pass through the filter stay in the circulation. The filtrate contains useful substances as well as waste, so filtering is only the first stage.

sources: Nephron Structure and Function / Function of a Nephron / Reabsorption and Secretion
units.text: After filtration, the kidney takes useful water and dissolved substances back from the tubule into the blood. This is reabsorption. Secretion moves substances in the other direction, from blood into the tubular fluid. Hormones help regulate what is reabsorbed and secreted, which supports the balance of water and mineral salts.

Innate immunity is the body's built-in defence against a broad range of potential pathogens. It usually acts very rapidly and includes physical, chemical and cellular defences. These parts overlap and work together. They are not impenetrable: pathogens can sometimes get past them, and an immune response can also contribute to tissue damage.

Adaptive immunity targets particular pathogens and develops memory after an initial exposure, including exposure through a vaccine. A later response to that same pathogen can be faster and stronger. B cells make antibodies, while T cells have several roles, including coordinating responses and destroying infected cells. This memory is specific: protection against one virus does not automatically protect against another.

Think of innate immunity as the built-in defences that respond rapidly to many potential pathogens. Adaptive immunity targets particular pathogens and can respond faster on a later encounter because of specific immune memory. They are connected systems: innate defences include barriers and cellular responses; adaptive responses involve B and T lymphocytes. Neither description means every exposure will be prevented.

sources: Sliding Filament Theory of Muscle Contraction
units.text: In skeletal muscle, myosin repeatedly attaches to and pulls on actin. The filaments slide past one another, pulling the ends of each sarcomere closer together. A sarcomere is a repeating unit inside a muscle fibre; as these units shorten, the muscle contracts. This is the sliding filament explanation of contraction.

sources: Sliding Filament Theory of Muscle Contraction / Crossbridge Cycling
units.text: A crossbridge forms when a myosin head binds to actin. Its power stroke pulls the actin inward. Binding a new ATP molecule lets myosin detach; splitting ATP supplies energy to reposition the head so another cycle can begin. ATP therefore matters for both detachment and preparation for the next cycle.

sources: 4.1 Glycolysis and the Pyruvate Dehydrogenase Complex (PDC)
units.text: Glycolysis breaks down glucose into two pyruvate molecules. It has an early energy-investment phase and a later energy-producing phase; the net yield is two ATP and two NADH per glucose. When oxygen delivery cannot meet energy demand, pyruvate can be converted to lactate, allowing NADH to be oxidised back to NAD so glycolysis can continue. This lactate-producing route yields much less energy than aerobic oxidation.
qualifications: when oxygen delivery cannot meet energy demand

sources: 1.2 Enzyme Kinetics / Enzyme regulation / Competitive and noncompetitive inhibition
units.text: In the reversible competitive inhibition model described here, an inhibitor competes with the substrate for the enzyme's active site. More substrate is needed to reach a half-maximal rate, so apparent Km rises. Enough substrate can overcome that competition, so Vmax is unchanged. The qualification matters: this explanation concerns the reversible competitive model.

Fertilisation joins an egg and a sperm to form a zygote. Each contributes one set of chromosomes, producing a diploid genome. Mechanisms at the egg help prevent additional sperm from entering; entry of multiple sperm is called polyspermy and disrupts normal development.

Cardiac output is the volume of blood the heart pumps in one minute. The breathing chapter uses it as an analogy for minute ventilation, which is the volume of air moved in one minute. These quantities describe different systems: blood flow through the circulation and airflow through the lungs. This cited section defines cardiac output but does not cover its full regulation.

Epidemiology studies health events in populations: how they are distributed, what influences them, and how that knowledge can help control health problems. Its focus is the health of a community or population. It includes studying disease patterns and applying the findings to public health action.

sources: Section 2: Morbidity Frequency Measures / Definition of incidence proportion
units.text: Incidence proportion asks: of the people who were initially free of the disease, what proportion developed it during a specified period? It is also called cumulative incidence or risk. The time period and initially disease-free population must be stated; a count of new cases alone is not the complete measure.

sources: Section 2: Morbidity Frequency Measures / Definition of incidence rate
units.text: Incidence rate counts new cases in relation to the total person-time at risk. Each participant contributes the time they were observed before disease onset or another study endpoint. The denominator is the accumulated time for all participants, rather than simply the number of people.

sources: Section 2: Morbidity Frequency Measures / Definition of prevalence
units.text: Prevalence is the proportion of a population with a disease or attribute at a stated point or over a stated period. It includes both existing and new cases. Incidence is limited to new cases. Point prevalence describes a particular date; period prevalence describes an interval.

Depression is different from the passing sadness everyone can experience. It can affect feelings, thinking and everyday activities such as sleeping, eating or working. Genetic, biological, environmental and psychological factors can play a role. It can occur alongside other illnesses, and the conditions can affect one another. This is an explanation of the condition, not a diagnosis of someone's symptoms.

sources: Bipolar Disorder / What is bipolar disorder?
units.text: Bipolar disorder involves mood episodes that can be much more extreme than ordinary ups and downs. Manic episodes include unusually elevated or irritable mood with increased activity; depressive episodes involve low mood and reduced functioning. Some people have hypomania, which is less severe than mania. Symptoms can come and go, and treatment can improve functioning and quality of life.

Schizophrenia affects how a person thinks, feels and behaves. Symptoms can make daily activities difficult and can be distressing for the person and their family. Effective treatments are available and can help people study, work, maintain relationships and become more independent. A brief description cannot establish an individual diagnosis.

For genetic testing, informed consent means understanding the procedure, benefits, limitations and possible consequences, then agreeing voluntarily. Possible false positives, false negatives, uninformative results, privacy and implications for relatives belong in that discussion. A person can change their mind after signing, before testing proceeds. This reference describes genetic-testing consent in a US educational context; Indian legal requirements need an applicable Indian source.
